questions.stem: A biology class displays the Indian variety of the pitcher plant, Nepenthes khasiana, and the teacher says that it grows naturally nowhere else on Earth. What is such a species called?

questions.subject: Science
questions.stem: A field survey records two regions. Region A holds a large number of species found nowhere else naturally, but no loss of its natural vegetation has been recorded. Region B holds a large number of such species and has lost a considerable part of its habitat. Which region is a biodiversity hotspot, and what must a region satisfy to be called one?

markingPoints.description: Region B is the biodiversity hotspot
A region must support a large number of endemic species and have undergone significant habitat loss

answerScheme.modelAnswer: Region B; it must support a large number of endemic species and have undergone significant habitat loss.

evidence:
Regions that support a large number of
endemic species and have undergone significant
habitat loss are known as biodiversity hotspots.

questions.subject: Science
questions.stem: A district officer proposes widening a road through a large forest area. Apart from the rare species it shelters, state two reasons why the forest deserves protection.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: It supports food webs; it helps ecosystems remain healthy.

questions.subject: Science
questions.stem:
While on a visit to a wildlife sanctuary, Tanya learns that the Lion-tailed macaque and the Neelakurinji plant occur only in India and nowhere else naturally. A forestry officer then tells her that four such regions have been identified in the country: the Western Ghats, Indo-Burma, the Himalayas and Sundaland. He explains that a region is called a biodiversity hotspot only when it holds a large number of species found nowhere else and has also lost a lot of its natural habitat. Sundaland, he adds, includes the Nicobar Islands. Tanya notes that these regions hold a great variety of organisms and keep the whole ecosystem working.

(a) What is the name for species that occur only in one region of the world and are found nowhere else naturally? (b) Name the two conditions a region must satisfy to be called a biodiversity hotspot, and name the hotspot that includes the Nicobar Islands. (c) Tanya feels that saving species found nowhere else is reason enough to protect these regions. Using what she has learnt, give one further reason why protecting them is equally important.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) They are called endemic species. (b) A region must support a large number of endemic species and have undergone significant habitat loss; Sundaland includes the Nicobar Islands. (c) These areas are rich in number and in the diversity of organisms; they support food webs and help ecosystems remain healthy.

questions.subject: Science
questions.stem:
Neha's geography project is on the natural landscape of India. She writes that the country is not uniform at all: there are mountains in the north, desert in the west, rainforests in the North East India, and long coastlines along the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal. She also learns that each such region has its own soil type and its own temperature and rainfall. Her guide points out that no two of these places are alike, and that together they are able to support a wide variety of species.

(a) Name the two climatic conditions that vary from one region of India to another. (b) Name the two seas along which the long coastline of the country runs. (c) Neha wonders why a student living in the desert and a student living in the North East India may see quite different plants and animals. Using the diversity of the landscape, explain why these habitats can support a wide variety of species.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) Temperature and rainfall. (b) The Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal. (c) Each region has distinct soil types and different climatic conditions, so these diverse habitats together support a wide variety of species.

questions.subject: Science
questions.stem:
Rohit's biology club takes a field trip to four of India's biodiversity hotspots. The guide lists them as the Western Ghats, Indo-Burma including North East India, the Himalayas, and Sundaland including the Nicobar Islands. When Rohit asks what all four have in common, the guide replies that each of them supports a large number of endemic species, has lost a considerable part of its habitat, and is rich in both the number and the diversity of the organisms living there. Rohit also spots a Neelakurinji plant in bloom and is told that it grows naturally in no other country in the world.

(a) Name any two of the four hotspots that the guide lists. (b) What two features do all four share, one about species and one about habitat? (c) Rohit feels that saving species found nowhere else in the world is reason enough to protect these areas. Based on what the guide said, give one further reason why protecting them matters.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) Any two, for example the Western Ghats and the Himalayas. (b) Each supports a large number of endemic species and has undergone significant habitat loss. (c) These areas are rich in number and in the diversity of organisms, so losing them would mean losing a great deal of biodiversity.

questions.subject: Science
questions.topic: Some criteria to classify living organisms
questions.stem:
While making a nature scrapbook, Ishan collects four organisms: a green plant, a fish, a mushroom and a worm. His teacher asks him to sort them into groups instead of guessing from how they look. She points out that an organism can be judged by its mode of nutrition, by its cell structure, and by the role it plays in the ecosystem as a producer, a consumer or a decomposer. She also mentions that some features cannot be seen at all and have to be studied through DNA. Ishan wonders whether two organisms that look completely different could still be related.

(a) Name the criterion whose features cannot be seen and must be studied in detail using DNA. (b) Ishan's two organisms look completely different. Explain what similar inherited features in them would suggest about their past, and state one criterion on which they could still be compared.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) Genetic similarity; scientists study it in detail using DNA. (b) Similar features suggest that they have evolved from common ancestors. They could still be compared on external features, mode of nutrition, cell structure or ecological role.
